accuracy.evidence: Every feeding link in the lab was checked against the RSPB and Woodland Trust species notes: rabbits graze grass, foxes take rabbits, caterpillars eat leaves, blue tits feed caterpillars to chicks, sparrowhawks take blue tits, song thrushes smash snails, cats take thrushes, tadpoles graze pondweed and algae, fish eat tadpoles and otters eat fish. Plants are called producers that make food from light, water and carbon dioxide (BBC Bitesize KS2 food chains); the Sun is named as the energy source but not as a link. Seaweed was swapped for a sunflower so the lab never calls an alga a plant.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the food-chain errors documented by Allen (2014) and the AAAS Project 2061 items: arrows read as 'eats' and drawn from eater to food, a chain started with the biggest animal or the Sun, plants that eat soil or drink their food from rain, a plant eater called a producer, and the belief that removing one population changes nothing or that a predator just switches to eating plants.

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab orders living things into a chain, flips arrows between them, sorts producer from consumer one organism at a time, removes a population and shows the knock-on effect, and fills the missing link of 4-step chains. None of that is the herbivore food-bowl sorter of 497 (flagdiet). The 6-token shingle gate passed against every other flag lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner must place the plant first before any animal is accepted, then discovers the arrow rule by turning red arrows green, then names producers and consumers, then sees the fox go hungry and the grass grow when rabbits vanish, then applies the plant-first rule to longer chains. Each completion line states the rule the task just showed, e.g. 'The arrow goes from the food to the eater.'

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions: what every chain starts with ('The biggest animal' tempts), which way the lettuce-snail arrow points ('From the snail to the lettuce' tempts, because the snail does the eating), and what happens to the fox when the rabbits go ('Nothing changes' and 'It eats the grass instead' tempt). The reveal line reports the guess against what the lab showed.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven questions with fourteen tagged slips (arrow, arrow2, big, sun, eatsplant, top, big2, home, nothing, switch, backward, middle, soil, rain). Each names the error with the question's own organisms, e.g. 'That is back to front: an owl does not feed seeds. Start with the plant: seeds → mouse → owl.' and 'Plants do not eat soil. They make food in their leaves using sunlight.'

readability.evidence: Kid text FK grade 1.5 and adult text 9.0, inside the 6.5 and 9.5 limits. Words are short and concrete for ages 6-7; producer and consumer are introduced with a plain gloss ('makes its own food', 'eats other living things'), and canvas prompts wrap onto two lines on a 360 px phone instead of shrinking.

no_filler.evidence: Passed the filler scan and the 12% explanation-overlap gate, including against 497 Herbivores, Carnivores and Omnivores. Each kid paragraph adds one idea (what a chain is, the arrow, producers and consumers, losing a link); the adult paragraphs give the NC Year 2 and NGSS wording, the science, named mistakes and the lab.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots on iPhone 13 light and Android 360 px dark, before and after Show me on every step: three or four creature circles fit across the width with names readable, tray cards are about 100 x 80 px for small fingers, every action has a full-width button twin under the canvas, and finished states show the completed chains rather than an empty stage.

accessibility.evidence: The browser gate ran axe WCAG 2.1 AA in light and dark on desktop and iPhone 13 with no violations and no console errors. Each canvas drag or tap has a button twin (Add grass, Turn arrow 1-3, Producer/Consumer, Take away the rabbit, Put in tadpole) and the canvas aria-label is rewritten with each spoken message.
